title: State and User Interaction
subtitle: Make Your App Alive - From Static to Dynamic
description: Master useState, how state triggers re-renders, events, interactive UIs. Build live progress tracking, like buttons, and unlock system for your dashboard.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: The Problem - Why Props Alone Is Not Enough

Hey! In Lesson 3 you made LessonCards dynamic with props. But they are still STATIC. If user completes Lesson 3, how does Lesson 4 automatically unlock? How does progress bar go from 20% to 30%? Props cannot change by themselves - props are read-only!

You need STATE. State = data that changes over time inside a component, and when it changes, React automatically re-renders that component. Props = data passed from parent (external). State = data managed inside component (internal) that can change.
Think: Props is like a letter you receive - you read it but cannot change it. State is like your mood - it changes, and your face (UI) changes automatically. Let's make your dashboard mood change!
Open Menu > Practical > React editor. We build live from Page 1.
PAGE 2: useState - Your First Interactive Component

useState is a Hook - a function that gives superpowers to functional components. Syntax: const [count, setCount] = useState(0). count = current value, setCount = function to change it, 0 = initial value. When you call setCount(1), React re-renders component with count=1.

blocks.title: Example 1: Counter - The Hello World of State

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You have a Like button for a post. Likes start at 10. When user clicks Like, likes should become 11 instantly without page reload. What do you use?
options: Props only - <LikeButton likes={10} />
State with useState - const [likes, setLikes] = useState(10) and setLikes(likes+1) on click
You need to reload the whole page
You cannot do instant updates in React
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! State is for data that changes with user interaction. Likes change, so it's state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Data that changes over time = State. Use useState for likes. Props cannot change by child.
blocks.reasoning: State manages changing UI data, props are for passing static/config data.

blocks.text: PAGE 3: Events - How User Actions Change State

User clicks button, types input, scrolls - these are events. In React you handle with onClick, onChange, onSubmit. Inside event handler you call setState function. Pattern: Event -> setState -> React re-renders -> UI updates. This loop is the heart of interactive apps.

PAGE 4: Why State Triggers Re-Render - The Magic

Critical question: Why not just do let count=0; count++? Why need useState? Because React doesn't know let variable changed! When you call setCount(), you are telling React: 'Hey, data changed, please re-render me!' React then calls your component function again with new state value and updates only changed DOM via Virtual DOM.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You used let status = 'locked'; status = 'current'; but UI didn't update. Why?
options: React only re-renders when you use setState from useState, not when you change a let variable
You need to refresh browser manually
let doesn't work in React at all
You need to use props
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! React watches only state changes via setState. let change is invisible to React.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: React re-render is triggered ONLY by setState (or props change from parent). let variable change doesn't trigger re-render.
blocks.reasoning: Understanding re-render mechanism is crucial for debugging.

blocks.text: PAGE 5: Multiple States & Objects in State

You can have many useState in one component. Also state can be object, array, not just number. For your dashboard you might need: completedCount, currentLessonId, xp, coins - 4 states! Or one object state with all.

blocks.title: Example 4: Your Real App State - XP, Coins, Progress

blocks.question: APPLICATION: In your navbar you show XP and Coins (stat-pill). User completes lesson, XP should go from 0 to 100, coins 0 to 20. How?
options: Use props only in navbar
Use useState in parent App for xp and coins, pass to Navbar as props, update state when lesson completes
Hardcode XP as 0 always
You need backend database for XP
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Parent holds state, passes to children as props. When state updates, Navbar props update, UI updates. Props + State combo!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Parent App holds xp state, passes to Navbar via props. When lesson completed, setXp(xp+50) -> Navbar re-renders with new XP.
blocks.reasoning: Lifting state up + props down is core pattern for shared data like XP.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You want a search bar in your React course page to filter lessons by title. User types 'hooks', only Hooks lessons show. How?
options: Use state for search text, onChange updates search state, filter lessons array using search state

blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! search state + onChange + filter + map = live search. You'll build this in Lesson 7 too!

blocks.reasoning: Input state pattern is foundation for forms and filtering.

blocks.text: PAGE 8: Lifting State Up - Sharing State Between Components

Your LessonCard needs to tell App that lesson is completed so App can update progress bar and XP. But LessonCard is child, App is parent. How? LIFT STATE UP: Put state in parent App, pass state and setState function as props to children. Children call function prop to update parent state. This is the most important pattern for your final app!

blocks.question: APPLICATION: Your dashboard has Navbar showing XP and LessonGrid showing cards. Both need same completed count. Where should completed state live?
options: Inside Navbar only
Inside LessonCard only
In parent App - lifted up, then pass as prop to both Navbar and LessonGrid
State cannot be shared between components
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Lift state to common parent App, share via props to both Navbar and LessonGrid. That's how real apps share data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: When two components need same data, lift state to their closest common parent App.
blocks.reasoning: Lifting state up is solution for shared state between siblings.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Summary & Next Steps

You mastered today: useState syntax [value, setValue], why let doesn't trigger re-render but setState does, events onClick/onChange -> setState -> re-render loop, multiple states (xp, coins, completed), object/array state with lessons array, lifting state up to parent App to share between Navbar and LessonGrid, and function props to let child update parent state. Your dashboard is now INTERACTIVE, not static!

blocks.question: FINAL APPLICATION: User completes Lesson 4. You need to: 1) Mark Lesson 4 as completed 2) Unlock Lesson 5 to current 3) Add 50 XP 4) Update progress bar from 60% to 80% 5) Update navbar XP. How many states need to update and where?
options: Update only one state inside LessonCard
Update lessons array state (for status), xp state, coins state in parent App - one handleComplete function updates all, props pass new values to Navbar and ProgressBar which auto re-render
You need to manually edit HTML file
State cannot update multiple things at once
blocks.correctFeedback: BINGO! One function in parent App updates lessons, xp, coins states together. Child components receive new props and re-render automatically. That's the full flow towards Lesson 10 target!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Parent App holds lessons, xp, coins states. handleComplete does setLessons + setXp + setCoins together. All children re-render with new props.
blocks.reasoning: State lifting + multiple setStates + props down = interactive app architecture.
